title: Expert damages: Counterfactuals require grounded calculations
desc: Treats methodological reliability, breach and loss as separate issues, offering no AI-specific admissibility or disclosure rule.

kps.k: The supplied Matter of Weber material concerns the factual and methodological reliability of expert evidence, not an established AI-specific admissibility or disclosure rule.
kps.d: Despite the entity label, the excerpts do not establish a Frye gate, an affirmative duty to disclose AI-generated evidence, or priority as the first US ruling of that kind. They describe a trust-accounting dispute and the court’s criticism of an expert’s assumptions and calculations. The supported theme is that expert analysis requires a sound legal basis and factual foundation; attributing these defects to AI would go beyond the supplied record.

kps.k: The court distinguishes concerns about fiduciary conduct from proof of breach and resulting loss.
kps.d: The court applies a lay-trustee standard and places the burden of proving misconduct and causally related damages on the beneficiary. It gives greater latitude to retaining inherited assets than to purchasing new investments, rejects the expert’s proposed 10% concentration ceiling, and notes that retention did not prevent beneficiary support. Although it questions the trustee’s credibility and regards extended personal stays as potentially inappropriate, missing travel, work and rental records prevent findings of misconduct and measurable damages. The outcome therefore does not amount to an unqualified endorsement of the trustee’s conduct.

kps.k: The parties dispute the damages measure, but the court treats damages as an alternative issue after finding no proven breach.
kps.d: The beneficiary seeks hypothetical investment profits from an earlier sale; the trustee advocates comparing property cost with net sale proceeds. The court finds damages unnecessary to resolve, distinguishes the conduct from Rothko’s intentional self-dealing, and alternatively finds no attributable capital loss because the property generated an overall profit. Separately, the beneficiary fails to establish when an earlier sale could have occurred. These qualifications limit any reading of the decision as a general rejection of lost-profit claims.

qs.q: Testimony of Charles Ranson and Damages Calculations**  Objectant argues that in evaluating the Cat Island Property, the correct formula for damages is the "lost profit" standard due to the Petitioner's breach of fiduciary duties — in this case, the value of the sale proceeds of the Cat Island Property had it been sold and the proceeds reinvested in traditional securities.
qs.a: Matter of Weber — first US ruling imposing a Frye gate and affirmative disclosure duty on AI-generated evidence · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Petitioner argues for the "lost capital" standard — in this case, the difference between the total cost of the Cat Island Property and the final net sales price.
qs.a: Matter of Weber — first US ruling imposing a Frye gate and affirmative disclosure duty on AI-generated evidence · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The practical lesson concerns grounded counterfactuals and transparent calculations, rather than a technology-specific compliance requirement.
kps.d: The court identifies an outdated statutory basis, an analysis starting more than three years too early, omitted expenses and tax benefits, and inadequate treatment of distributions and actual sale proceeds. It rejects an assumed Vanguard investment as speculative and recommends comparison with the trust’s actual investment funds. It also criticizes omitting the analysis the expert described as industry-standard because of cost. For practitioners, these criticisms point to checking legal premises, establishing feasible alternative transactions, reconciling calculations with actual cash flows, and supporting assumptions with relevant expertise and historical evidence.

qs.q: Ranson cited to an outdated version of New York's Prudent Investor Act to support this proposition, further calling into question his credibility.
qs.a: Matter of Weber — first US ruling imposing a Frye gate and affirmative disclosure duty on AI-generated evidence · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Ranson's damages analysis were also calculated from a start date of December 31, 2004, which as set forth above, is more than three (3) years too early.
qs.a: Matter of Weber — first US ruling imposing a Frye gate and affirmative disclosure duty on AI-generated evidence · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: The court source supports the proposition that expert damages counterfactuals require legally and factually grounded, transparent calculations, while breach and resulting loss must be established separately. It rejects the expert’s analysis because it relied on an incorrect timeframe, omitted material cash flows and benefits, and used a speculative proxy investment rather than the trust’s actual investments. Material nuance is that the decision does not categorically reject lost-profit damages or counterfactual modelling: damages were unnecessary after no breach was proved, and the court indicated how a better-grounded comparison could have been constructed. Nor does the supplied decision establish an AI-specific Frye gate or disclosure duty. Because this facet contains one curated court source, it shows that decision’s reasoning rather than the prevalence of a broader judicial or regulatory view.

elens.an: The source directly supports the proposition for the 2023–2024 period. It treats breach, causation and damages as distinct questions and rejects the expert’s counterfactual damages analysis because it relied on defective legal premises, an incorrect start date, omitted actual cash flows and benefits, unsupported assumptions, and a speculative investment proxy. Its constructive methodological lesson is that counterfactuals should be transparent and anchored in feasible transactions and the trust’s actual investments. Materially, the decision does not create an AI-specific Frye gate or disclosure duty; nothing in the supplied evidence attributes the defects to AI. It also does not categorically reject lost-profit damages: damages were unnecessary after no breach was proved, and the court addressed them only in the alternative. This assessment concerns this curated source alone and does not indicate how prevalent the view was during the period.
